chunks: From him, from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan, from Amr ibn Sa'id, from Musaddiq ibn Sadah, from 'Ammar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

He was asked about a man who leads a group in prayer: is it permissible for him to wear a sash? He said, 'No, no. A man does not lead a group in prayer while wearing a sash over his clothes, even if he is wearing many clothes, because it is not permissible for the Imam to pray while wearing a sash.'

And about a man who catches the Imam at the time of the final salam (conclusion of prayer): He said, 'He must give the adhan, call the iqamah, and begin the prayer (with the opening takbir and recitation).'

key_terms.سَلَّمَ: the final salam (greeting) concluding the prayer
key_terms.يَتَوَشَّحَ: to wear a sash or girdle
key_terms.يُؤَذِّنَ: to give the adhan (call to prayer)
key_terms.يُقِيمَ: to call the iqamah (second call to prayer)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on an Imam wearing a sash during prayer, and what should a latecomer do if they catch the Imam after the final salam?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies two practical aspects of congregational prayer: the prohibition of the Imam wearing an outer sash (*tawashshuh*) to maintain dignity and uniformity, and the specific protocol for latecomers who miss the Imam's *salam*. The latter ruling emphasizes that joining late requires re-establishing the prayer's formalities through *adhan* and *iqamah*, reflecting the Shia emphasis on the structural integrity of the prayer unit. These details highlight the meticulous attention to ritual propriety (*adab*) in leading and participating in communal worship.
